solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: For whom one might provide perfect meal?

definitions.text: For whom one might provide perfect meal?

parts.note: the surface reads 'one' as a cook or host; the setter means 'one' is the person who provides the meal by being it
the question mark warns that the meal is a person, and the diner is someone who eats people

explanation.surface: A host wonders which guest would most appreciate a perfect dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'one might provide' as cooking for someone and nothing is cryptic; read it as 'one might BE the meal provided' and only a cannibal fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: to a people-eater, any person ('one') is the ideal meal, so the whole clue defines the diner.

clue.text: Fashionable way to make a Martini?

definitions.meaning: an informal phrase for trendy, up to date
It is short for Italian vermouth, as in the bar order gin and It

explanation.surface: A trendy barman explains the stylish way to mix a Martini.
explanation.walkthrough: IT is short for Italian vermouth, as in the old British bar order 'gin and It'; a Martini is gin made WITH IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the dated slang for up to date, and literally mixing gin with It, the Italian vermouth in a Martini.

clue.text: English atheist wrong to hang back

indicators.note: the letters are put together wrongly, so rearrange them

explanation.surface: An English unbeliever is thought mistaken for holding back from something.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'English atheist' as one person in the surface, but it splits into E plus the seven letters of ATHEIST to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe pausing, reluctant to act, and the verb swaps straight into 'to hang back'.

clue.text: Learn from the archdeacon

indicators.note: the answer is taken out from the words that follow

explanation.surface: A cleric passes on news learned from a senior churchman.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans the gap between two words: the end of 'the' and the start of 'archdeacon'.
explanation.definitionFit: The 'find out' sense, as in 'I hear you've moved', where being told is learning.

clue.text: Pest made off in a rush

indicators.note: the letters go off, out of their order

explanation.surface: A nuisance of a person dashes away in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made off' looks like a phrasal verb meaning fled; split it and 'made' is fodder while 'off' does the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun synonym: a headlong rush of cattle or a panicking crowd.

clue.text: Office worker briefly allowed place of worship

indicators.note: cut short, so the last letter of the word goes

parts.note: a temporary worker from an agency

explanation.surface: A temporary office worker is permitted some time at a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' sits before 'allowed' and shortens it, not the time the worker is given.
explanation.definitionFit: A general term covering the building of many faiths, Hindu, Jewish or ancient Greek.

clue.text: Sharp smell of insect rising

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top

explanation.surface: Something pungent wafts off a swarm of flying insects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' works because this is a down clue: an upward reading turns GNAT round.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, used of both smells and tastes, like the tang of sea air.

clue.text: US state welcoming Republican soldier

indicators.note: the state takes the letter in, as a host welcomes a guest

explanation.surface: A New England state gives a warm reception to a GOP soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pairs the state with a soldier, but the soldier is the definition and the state is only the outside shell.
explanation.definitionFit: A marine is a soldier who serves at sea with a navy, so the general word fits.

clue.text: Nearly everyone preparing for war is frightening

indicators.note: not quite all of the word, so its last letter goes

explanation.surface: Almost the whole nation readying itself for conflict is a scary prospect.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a sentence whose last word is the definition, with 'is' joining it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain adjective synonym: both describe what causes fear or alarm.

clue.text: Make very slow progress in church

parts.note: used as itself. The same letters also run on unbroken across neighbouring clue words, a coincidence of the pieces sitting side by side; the setter gives no hidden-word signal.

explanation.surface: A congregation shuffles slowly up the aisle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link word placing the progress inside a church, but it is a piece of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb from the unit of length: to move forward a tiny distance at a time.

clue.text: Friend in city across the pond quietly heading west

indicators.note: in an across entry, west is leftward, so read right to left

parts.note: LA = Los Angeles; 'across the pond' means in America

explanation.surface: A friend living in an American city moves quietly westward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Across the pond' is British slang for the United States, the Atlantic being the pond.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal synonym for a friend or mate.

clue.text: Clumsy bishop locates impediment

indicators.note: the letters are handled clumsily and fall out of order

parts.note: B = bishop, as in chess notation

explanation.surface: An awkward churchman finally finds what is in his way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locates' reads as the verb joining wordplay to definition, but it is fodder; the definition is simply the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain noun synonym: anything that blocks the way forward.

clue.text: University caterer cooking chicken?

indicators.note: the letters are cooked, stirred into a new form

explanation.surface: A college caterer is busy roasting chicken for the dining hall.
explanation.walkthrough: The kitchen surface makes chicken food, but here it is a living animal; the question mark says a chicken is just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a chicken is one kind of living being, flagged by the question mark.

clue.text: Almost get rid of Times

indicators.note: not quite the whole word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: ERASE (get rid of) without its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone nearly scraps their subscription to the Times newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital T disguises 'Times' as the newspaper; capitals may mislead, and here it is plain periods of history.
explanation.definitionFit: A plural synonym for periods of history, as in 'in Victorian times'.

clue.text: Dislike author's initial adaptation

indicators.note: the initial of a word is its first letter

parts.note: a new form of a work, such as a film of a novel

explanation.surface: A writer hates the first attempt at turning their book into a film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dislike' reads as a verb in the surface, but the answer is the noun, a strong dislike.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun synonym: a strong feeling of dislike or distaste.

clue.text: Fat female dog

explanation.surface: An overweight bitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat female dog' reads as one overweight animal, but the adjective is the definition, standing for a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal noun for fat, meaning the soft loose kind that wobbles on the body.

clue.text: Bet on the French acquiring European vehicle

indicators.note: BET takes in the letter, acquiring it
in a down entry, one piece written on another follows it

explanation.surface: A gambler wagers on French rivals picking up a European car.
explanation.walkthrough: The Volkswagen Beetle is the classic German car, so 'European vehicle' seems one idea; 'European' only supplies E.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by type: the Volkswagen car of that name, nicknamed for its rounded shape.

clue.text: Very happy to catch EV up

explanation.surface: An electric-vehicle owner is thrilled to catch up with another EV.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch up' looks like one phrase; split it and 'up' is the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Raised to a height, the sense of up in 'the platform is up off the ground'.

clue.text: Tempt a couple of learners to go on river

indicators.note: in a down entry, the first pieces go on top of the river

parts.note: the Ure, a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Two driving pupils are lured into a boating trip.
explanation.walkthrough: L for learner comes from the L-plates British learner drivers display. The Ure is a Yorkshire river, a crossword regular.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to entice someone with something attractive, as a lure draws fish.

clue.text: When one might expect to receive letter from Athens?

definitions.text: When one might expect to receive
definitions.meaning: the abbreviation for the estimated time of arrival
a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone wonders when a letter posted in Athens will arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about post, but the 'letter' is an alphabet letter, and the first half describes the time a delivery is due.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the estimated time of arrival tells you when to expect something, and eta is the seventh Greek letter.

clue.text: Dartmoor cave providing cover for hunter

indicators.note: the words cover the answer, which lies inside them

explanation.surface: A cave on the moor gives a hunter somewhere to hide.
explanation.walkthrough: Dartmoor is a moorland in Devon, so a hunter sheltering there sounds natural; the hunter is actually a sea creature.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the killer whale is a top predator of the ocean.

clue.text: Reportedly remitted money to America

indicators.note: as reported, spoken, so the sound counts, not the spelling

explanation.surface: Someone is said to have wired funds to the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Money to America' is the definition read as 'money, to an American': a cent is a US coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example with a regional tag: a coin in American money, one hundredth of a dollar.

clue.text: Fail nothing in London School of Economics

indicators.note: the letter goes in the abbreviation

explanation.surface: A student at the London School of Economics fails with zero marks.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface places a failure at the college; in the wordplay the college initials simply wrap the zero.
explanation.definitionFit: An intransitive verb sense: to fail to win, as a team does when it loses.

clue.text: Puritan concealing rubbish project

parts.note: a prim, strait-laced person, around ROT after its P

explanation.surface: A prim moralist hides a worthless scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Project' sits at the end looking like a noun, a scheme; it is the verb, to stick out.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb synonym, with project said pro-JECT: to jut out beyond a surface.

clue.text: Strict new school in the East End

indicators.note: Cockneys of London's East End drop the H from the start of words

parts.note: HARROW, a famous English boarding school, with the H dropped

explanation.surface: A newly founded school in the East of London is run on strict lines.
explanation.walkthrough: Harrow is a famous English private school; the East End is working-class London, whose Cockney speakers traditionally drop H, so Harrow becomes 'Arrow.
explanation.definitionFit: The limited, rigid sense, as in a narrow interpretation of a rule.

clue.text: Vulgar soldiers head for the lowest level

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Rough troops march down to the bottom floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head for' reads as a verb of movement, so the soldiers seem to be heading downstairs; it takes the first letter of 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: the floor of a building below ground, beneath all the others.
